library(multiScaleR)
library(terra)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(

  comment  = "#>",

  fig.height = 4.25,

# Slow steps (optimization, likelihood profiles, raster projection) are stored
# in the package so the vignette builds quickly. The text shows the real calls.
# Regenerate the stored results with data-raw/generate_vignette_cache.R.
cache_file <- file.path("..", "inst", "extdata", "vignette_cache.rds")
if (!file.exists(cache_file)) {

```

# What multiScaleR does

`multiScaleR` estimates the scale of effect, or the distance over which a
landscape variable influences an ecological response measured at survey
locations. You do not test a fixed set of buffer radii. Instead, the package
weights the landscape around each survey point with a distance-decay kernel and
estimates the kernel width, sigma, as a parameter of your regression model. You
get a scale estimate with a standard error and confidence interval, alongside
the familiar regression coefficients.

This guide takes about ten minutes. It fits one count model to data bundled
with the package and shows how to read every result. It assumes you can fit a
generalized linear model with `glm()` and have used `terra` to read a raster.
When you finish, the table in [Where to go next] points to the vignette for
your next question.

# Install the package

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("multiScaleR")
```

# The workflow in four steps

Every `multiScaleR` analysis follows the same four steps.

1. **Prepare the inputs** with `kernel_prep()`. This extracts the raster values
   around each survey point and stores what the optimizer needs.
2. **Fit a starting model** with an ordinary regression function such as
   `glm()`. The model formula and family carry through to the next step.
3. **Estimate the scales of effect** with `multiScale_optim()`. This finds the
   sigma for each landscape covariate and the regression coefficients that
   together maximize the model likelihood.
4. **Read and map the results** with `summary()`, `plot()`,
   `plot_marginal_effects()`, `profile_sigma()`, and `kernel_scale.raster()`.

# Work through an example

## Load the data

The package includes a simulated data set of counts at 100 survey locations and
a raster with three landscape layers.

```{r load-data}
data("landscape_counts")   # data frame: counts and one site-level covariate
dat <- landscape_counts

data("surv_pts")           # survey locations (an sf object from the package)
pts <- vect(surv_pts)      # convert to a terra SpatVector

# Three landscape layers on one grid, in meters
land_rast <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                              package = "multiScaleR"))
```

The counts were simulated from known values, which lets you check each estimate
against the truth later in this guide.

| Quantity | True value |
|:---------|:-----------|
| Scale of effect (sigma) for `land1`, a binary habitat layer | 250 m |
| Scale of effect (sigma) for `land2`, a continuous layer | 500 m |
| Effect of `land1` on log expected count | -0.5 |
| Effect of `land2` on log expected count | 0.7 |
| Effect of `site`, a covariate measured at the survey point | 0.3 |
| `land3`, a continuous layer | No effect |

```{r plot-data, fig.cap = "***The three landscape layers, and the survey points over `land1`.***"}
plot(land_rast)
plot(land_rast$land1, main = "land1 with survey points")
points(pts, pch = 19, cex = 0.6, col = "red")
```

## Prepare the kernel inputs

`kernel_prep()` extracts the raster values within `max_D` map units of each
survey point and computes a first set of distance-weighted covariate values.
The map units here are meters.

```{r kernel-prep}
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(
  pts          = pts,          # survey locations
  raster_stack = land_rast,    # landscape layers to summarize
  max_D        = 1700,         # largest distance (m) considered around a point
  kernel       = "gaussian",   # shape of the distance-decay function
  verbose      = FALSE
)
```

**Choosing `max_D`:** Set `max_D` to a distance you are confident exceeds the
true scale of effect. If you are unsure, err toward a larger value, because the
optimizer can only search within that distance. The cost is computation, since
a larger `max_D` means more raster cells to process. If `multiScale_optim()`
later warns that a sigma estimate is close to `max_D`, increase `max_D` and run
`kernel_prep()` again.

The kernel-weighted covariates are in `kernel_inputs$kernel_dat`, one row per
survey point. They are centered and scaled, so each has a mean of zero and a
standard deviation of one. Combine them with the response data.

```{r build-df}
df <- data.frame(dat, kernel_inputs$kernel_dat)
head(df, 3)
```

## Fit a starting model

Fit the regression model you intend to optimize. `multiScale_optim()` inherits
the formula and family from this model, so settle the model structure here. The
coefficients at this stage are only starting values, because the landscape
covariates were weighted with a first guess at sigma.

```{r fit-mod}
mod <- glm(counts ~ site + land1 + land2,
           family = poisson(),
           data   = df)
```

## Estimate the scales of effect

`multiScale_optim()` searches over sigma for each landscape covariate, refits
the regression at each candidate, and keeps the combination with the highest
likelihood.

```{r optim, eval = FALSE}
opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod    = mod,
                        kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs)
```

```{r load-cached-opt, include = FALSE}
opt <- vignette_cache$quickstart$opt
# The stored fit was produced by this same call under different object names.
# Show the call as it is written above.
opt$call <- quote(multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = mod,
                                   kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs))
```

Larger problems can run in parallel with `n_cores`, which needs more memory.
`estimate_multiscale_ram()` reports how much. If a model has several landscape
covariates and the result seems sensitive to its starting values, see the
screened-start option in `vignette("multiScaleR_Guide", package = "multiScaleR")`.

## Read the summary

```{r summary}
summary(opt)
```

**How to read the `summary()` output:** The output has four parts.

- **Optimized Scale of Effect.** One row per landscape covariate, with the
  estimated sigma in map units (meters here), its standard error, and a 95%
  confidence interval.
- **Optimized Scale of Effect, Distance.** Sigma is a kernel parameter, not a
  radius. This block converts it to an effective distance. The first table,
  marked "selected", gives the radius of the circle that holds 90% of the
  kernel weight. Report this distance when you describe how far the landscape
  effect extends. The second table is an older, line-based definition kept for
  comparison.
- **Fitted Model Summary.** The regression table from the final model. For this
  Poisson model the coefficients are on the log scale, so exponentiate them to
  get a multiplicative change in the expected count.
- **Follow-up recommendation.** Starting values and a `max_D` to reuse if you
  refit the model.

The lines below pull those quantities out of the fitted object.

```{r read-summary}
est     <- summary(opt)$opt_scale          # sigma, SE, and 95% interval (m)
dist90  <- kernel_dist(opt)                # radius holding 90% of kernel weight (m)
effects <- exp(coef(opt$opt_mod))          # multiplicative change in expected count

round(dist90)
round(effects, 2)
```

Three statements follow from these numbers.

- The estimated sigma for `land1` is `r round(est["land1", "Mean"])` m. A
  Gaussian kernel of that width places 90% of its weight within
  `r round(dist90["land1", "Mean"])` m of a survey point, so habitat within
  roughly that distance shapes the count.
- The estimated sigma for `land2` is `r round(est["land2", "Mean"])` m, an
  effective distance of `r round(dist90["land2", "Mean"])` m. `land2` acts over
  about twice the distance of `land1`.
- The landscape covariates are standardized, so each coefficient describes a
  change of one standard deviation. A one standard deviation increase in
  kernel-weighted `land1` multiplies the expected count by
  `r round(effects["land1"], 2)`, a decrease of
  `r round(100 * (1 - effects["land1"]))`%. The same increase in `land2`
  multiplies it by `r round(effects["land2"], 2)`, an increase of
  `r round(100 * (effects["land2"] - 1))`%.

Because the data are simulated, you can compare each estimate with its true
value.

```{r truth-table}
ci_beta <- confint.default(opt$opt_mod)    # Wald 95% intervals, log scale
check <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("sigma, land1 (m)", "sigma, land2 (m)",
                "effect of land1", "effect of land2", "effect of site"),
  Truth     = c(250, 500, -0.5, 0.7, 0.3),
  Estimate  = c(est[, "Mean"], coef(opt$opt_mod)[c("land1", "land2", "site")]),
  Lower     = c(est[, "2.5%"], ci_beta[c("land1", "land2", "site"), 1]),
  Upper     = c(est[, "97.5%"], ci_beta[c("land1", "land2", "site"), 2])
)
# Does each 95% interval contain the value used to simulate the data?
check$Covered <- check$Truth >= check$Lower & check$Truth <= check$Upper
knitr::kable(check, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

**How to read the table:** `Covered` is `TRUE` when the 95% interval contains
the true value. One simulated data set cannot show that the intervals are
reliable in general, but it does show what recovery looks like when the model
matches the process that generated the data.

> **What this means for your study.** Report the effective distance, not sigma
> alone, and say which weight it refers to (90% by default). The coefficient
> standard errors in the regression table treat the estimated sigma values as
> known. `vignette("inference-contracts", package = "multiScaleR")` explains
> what that leaves out and when it matters.

By default, the sigma intervals come from the optimizer's standard errors (the
delta method). When the sample is small or an estimate sits near `max_D`, request
profile-likelihood intervals with `summary(opt, profile = TRUE)`. They take
longer to compute and do not assume a symmetric likelihood.

## Plot the kernels and the covariate effects

```{r plot-kernel, fig.cap = "***Kernel weight against distance for each landscape covariate.***"}
plot(opt)
```

**How to read these plots:** Each curve shows how the weight given to a raster
cell declines with its distance from the survey point. The dashed line marks
the effective distance from `summary()`, the radius that holds 90% of the
kernel weight, and the gray band is its 95% confidence interval. The three
lines of text under each panel repeat sigma, that radius, and its interval. A
curve that falls quickly means the response depends on nearby landscape. A
curve that falls slowly means distant landscape still counts.

The text under each panel is useful while you explore a fit, but a figure for a
manuscript or a slide usually reads better without it. Set `add_label = FALSE`
to draw the same panels with no text beneath them. The dashed line and the gray
band stay.

```{r plot-kernel-plain, fig.cap = "***The same kernel plots without the text under each panel.***"}
plot(opt, add_label = FALSE)
```

Versions through 0.7.3 reported a line-based distance, which is shorter (about
1.65 sigma at 90% for a Gaussian kernel, against about 2.15 sigma for the
circle). Set `dimension = "1d"` in `summary()`, `plot()`, or `kernel_dist()` to
reproduce those earlier values. The fitted model is the same either way.

```{r marginal, fig.cap = "***Estimated effect of each covariate on the expected count.***"}
plot_marginal_effects(opt)
```

**How to read these plots:** Each panel shows the expected count across the
observed range of one covariate, with the other covariates held at their means.
The horizontal axis is in the covariate's own units. For `land1`, a binary
habitat layer, that is the kernel-weighted proportion of habitat around a
survey point. The shaded band is a 95% confidence band for the expected count.
The band treats the estimated scales as known, so it does not include
uncertainty in sigma. Set `add_label = TRUE` if you want that reminder printed
under each panel.

## Check that each scale is well identified

`profile_sigma()` refits the model across a range of sigma values for one
covariate at a time, holding the other scales at their estimates.

```{r profile-call, eval = FALSE}
prof <- profile_sigma(opt, n_pts = 15)   # 15 sigma values per covariate
plot(prof)
```

```{r profile, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "***AICc across candidate sigma values. The dashed line marks the estimate.***"}
prof <- vignette_cache$quickstart$prof
plot(prof)
```

**How to read these plots:** Lower AICc means better support. A clear trough
near the dashed line means the data identify that scale well. A flat profile,
or one that keeps falling toward the edge of the search range, means the data
say little about that scale, and its interval should be read with caution.

## Map the fitted model

`kernel_scale.raster()` applies each fitted kernel to the whole raster. With
`scale_center = TRUE` it also standardizes the result with the mean and
standard deviation used in fitting, so the layers can go straight into
`terra::predict()`.

```{r project-call, eval = FALSE}
r_scaled <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = land_rast,
                                multiScaleR  = opt,     # the fitted object
                                scale_center = TRUE,    # same scaling as the model
                                clamp        = TRUE)    # stay within the fitted range

# Expected count in every raster cell
pred <- terra::predict(r_scaled, opt$opt_mod, type = "response")
```

```{r project, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "***Landscape layers smoothed at their estimated scales, in standard deviation units.***"}
r_scaled <- terra::unwrap(vignette_cache$quickstart$r_scaled)
plot(r_scaled)
```

```{r predict, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "***Expected count across the landscape, with survey points.***"}
pred <- terra::unwrap(vignette_cache$quickstart$pred)
plot(pred, main = "Expected count")
points(pts, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "red")
```

**How to read these plots:** The first figure shows each landscape layer after
kernel weighting. Its values are in standard deviation units of the data used
to fit the model, so zero is the average survey point. The second figure is the
expected count per cell from the fitted model. With `clamp = TRUE`, cells whose
covariate values fall outside the range seen at the survey points are held at
the nearest observed value, which keeps the model from extrapolating.

Expected counts fall toward zero near the map border in this example. That
pattern reflects a small landscape combined with a large scale of effect for
`land2`, not an ecological result.
`vignette("spatial_projection_clamping", package = "multiScaleR")` covers
projection beyond the sampled conditions in detail.

# Quick reference

The full workflow in one block.

```{r full-workflow, eval = FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
library(terra)

# 1. Load the data
data("landscape_counts"); data("surv_pts")
pts       <- vect(surv_pts)
land_rast <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                              package = "multiScaleR"))

# 2. Prepare the kernel inputs
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast,
                             max_D = 1700, kernel = "gaussian")

# 3. Fit a starting model
df  <- data.frame(landscape_counts, kernel_inputs$kernel_dat)
mod <- glm(counts ~ site + land1 + land2, family = poisson(), data = df)

# 4. Estimate the scales of effect
opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = mod, kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs)

# 5. Read the results
summary(opt)                   # sigma, effective distance, regression table
summary(opt, profile = TRUE)   # profile-likelihood intervals for sigma (slower)
kernel_dist(opt)               # radius holding 90% of the kernel weight
exp(coef(opt$opt_mod))         # multiplicative change in expected count
plot(opt)                      # kernel weight against distance
plot(opt, add_label = FALSE)   # the same plot without the text beneath it
plot_marginal_effects(opt)     # expected count across each covariate
plot(profile_sigma(opt))       # AICc across sigma: is each scale identified?

# 6. Map the fitted model
r_scaled <- kernel_scale.raster(land_rast, multiScaleR = opt,
                                scale_center = TRUE, clamp = TRUE)
pred <- terra::predict(r_scaled, opt$opt_mod, type = "response")
```

## Summary of key functions

| Function | Purpose |
|:---------|:--------|
| `kernel_prep()` | Extract raster values around each survey point and prepare the optimizer inputs |
| `multiScale_optim()` | Estimate sigma for each landscape covariate together with the regression coefficients |
| `summary()` | Report sigma, the effective distance, and the regression table |
| `kernel_dist()` | Convert sigma to the distance that holds a chosen share of the kernel weight |
| `plot()` | Draw kernel weight against distance |
| `plot_marginal_effects()` | Draw the expected response across each covariate |
| `profile_sigma()` | Check how well the data identify each scale |
| `kernel_scale.raster()` | Apply the fitted kernels to a raster for mapping and prediction |
